About this citation

Socrates is the principal speaker. The dialogue's argument is conducted by the characters, and the archive therefore presents passages under Socrates while citing the work to Plato — the distinction the corpus's `author` field flattens.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“Justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in others'.”
Ancient Greek
“τὸ τὰ αὑτοῦ πράττειν καὶ μὴ πολυπραγμονεῖν δικαιοσύνη ἐστί.”

“Doing one's own things and not being a busybody is justice.” The archive's English compresses πολυπραγμονεῖν to “not meddling in others’.”

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in others'.”
  • “Justice is minding one's own business.”

Attribution notes

Plato, Republic IV 433a–b, where justice in the city is defined as each class doing its own work. The popular shortening “justice is minding one's own business” loses the institutional claim and reads as personal etiquette.

How to cite and check Plato quotations

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Republic IV 433a and files it under Platonism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Plato

Plato (c. 428/427–348/347 BCE) was an Athenian of high birth, a devoted associate of Socrates, and the founder of the Academy.

Interpretation

In the Republic this is a definition proposed in the course of building an ideal city, and it is deliberately narrow. Plato is not offering a theory of fairness between persons; he is describing a condition of a well-ordered whole in which each part performs its proper function without interfering with the others. Justice in a soul and justice in a city are the same structural property. The definition is incomplete by modern standards, which is part of why it generates the argument that follows.

Why it matters

It still gives a sharp diagnostic: much of what we call injustice is meddling — taking on what is not ours. Before asking whether a situation is fair, ask whether people are doing what is actually theirs to do.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Justice is doing one's own work and not…”?

“Justice is doing one's own work and not…” comes from Republic, IV 433a (c. 375 BCE), attributed to Plato.

What does Plato mean by justice?

Distributive, retributive, and restorative justice name different problems. Political philosophy asks what a just society owes its members and outsiders. This passage enters that discussion through justice, order, responsibility.

Is the wording of this Plato quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in others'.” Forms in circulation that differ: Justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in others'. / Justice is minding one's own business. The Ancient Greek reads “τὸ τὰ αὑτοῦ πράττειν καὶ μὴ πολυπραγμονεῖν δικαιοσύνη ἐστί.”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Plato, Republic IV 433a–b, where justice in the city is defined as each class doing its own work. The popular shortening “justice is minding one's own business” loses the institutional claim and reads as personal etiquette.
